segments.text: Chemistry begins with the atom, and modern atomic structure cannot be understood without quantum mechanics. This chapter sets the foundation for the entire subject: how electrons are arranged determines bonding (Chapter 8 onward), reactivity, and the periodic trends that organise all of inorganic and organic chemistry.

blocks.text: 1. Wave nature of matter and basic quantum concepts

segments.text: Just as de Broglie proposed that matter has an associated wavelength (λ = h/p, covered in Physics Chapter II), electrons in atoms must be described as standing waves rather than particles on fixed orbits. This wave nature is the reason electron energies in atoms are quantized — only specific “standing wave” patterns around the nucleus are self-consistent, analogous to only certain wavelengths fitting a vibrating string.

blocks.text: 2. The Schrödinger equation and interpretation of the wavefunction

segments.text: Solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation for an electron in the Coulomb potential of a nucleus gives both the allowed energy levels and the corresponding wavefunctions (

Each orbital is labelled by three quantum numbers arising naturally from solving the equation: principal (n = 1, 2, 3…, determines overall size/energy), azimuthal (l = 0 to n−1, determines shape: l=0 is s, spherical; l=1 is p, dumbbell-shaped; l=2 is d, more complex), and magnetic (mₗ, determines orientation in space). A fourth, spin (mₛ = ±½), comes from relativistic quantum mechanics and distinguishes the two electrons that can occupy any one spatial orbital.

Electrons in atoms are described by wavefunctions (orbitals) rather than fixed classical orbits; |ψ|² gives the probability of finding the electron at a location.
Four quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) specify each electron’s state; the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund’s rule together determine how electrons fill orbitals in an atom.

Periodic trends in atomic radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity follow directly from how effectively increasing nuclear charge and additional electron shells balance each other across the periodic table.
